purpose: Enalaprilat is used to treat high blood pressure, especially in situations where you need a medication given directly into your vein (intravenously) in a hospital setting. It helps bring down dangerously high blood pressure quickly when you cannot take a pill by mouth. It may also be used to help your heart work better if you have heart failure.
how_it_works: Your body makes a chemical called angiotensin II that causes your blood vessels to tighten and squeeze, which raises your blood pressure. Enalaprilat blocks an enzyme that your body needs to make that chemical. When that chemical is blocked, your blood vessels relax and open up, making it easier for your heart to pump blood and lowering your blood pressure.
common_side_effects: The most common side effects include dizziness, lightheadedness (especially when you stand up quickly), low blood pressure, headache, fatigue, and a dry nagging cough. Some people may also notice mild nausea or a feeling of weakness.
warnings: Do not use this medication if you are pregnant or planning to become pregnant, as it can seriously harm your unborn baby. Tell your doctor if you have ever had a severe allergic reaction called angioedema (swelling of the face, lips, tongue, or throat), as this can happen with ACE inhibitors. Let your doctor know if you have kidney problems, high potassium levels, or if you are taking potassium supplements or certain other blood pressure medicines. Since this is given in a hospital, medical staff will closely monitor your blood pressure and kidney function.
typical_dosing: Because this is a hospital medication given through an IV, a nurse or doctor will give it to you. The usual starting dose is 1.25 mg given slowly over 5 minutes into your vein, and this can be repeated every 6 hours as needed. Your medical team will adjust the dose based on how your blood pressure responds and how your kidneys are working.
